title: Given a bitonic array, strictly increasing then strictly decreasing, find the index of a given key. If the key appears on both sides, return the smaller index. Explain how you first find the peak and then binary-search each side with the correct order.
shortTitle: Search Bitonic Array (Find a Key in a Rise-Then-Fall Array)

s1_definition.profdef: Search Bitonic Array combines two Modified Binary Search ideas. First we find the peak index of the bitonic array. That peak splits the array into an ascending part on the left and a descending part on the right. We binary-search the ascending part normally, and if the key is not there we binary-search the descending part with reversed comparisons. Returning the first match gives the smaller index when the key appears twice.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the intraday price series of Rajesh's stock rises to a high then falls, and the compliance team asks at which point in the day the price first hit a specific value. We find the daily high, then search the rising half, and if not found there, search the falling half.
s1_definition.oneliner: Find the peak, binary-search the ascending left half, then if needed binary-search the descending right half, returning the earlier match.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Search Bitonic Array combines two Modified Binary Search ideas. First we find the peak index of the bitonic array. That peak splits the array into an ascending part on the left and a descending part on the right. We binary-search the ascending part normally, and if the key is not there we binary-search the descending part with reversed comparisons. Returning the first match gives the smaller index when the key appears twice.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the intraday price series of Rajesh's stock rises to a high then falls, and the compliance team asks at which point in the day the price first hit a specific value. We find the daily high, then search the rising half, and if not found there, search the falling half.

**One line to remember:** Find the peak, binary-search the ascending left half, then if needed binary-search the descending right half, returning the earlier match.

sections.s2_technical:
We first find the peak index with the Bitonic Maximum technique, comparing each middle with its right neighbour. Once we have `peak`, we run a standard ascending binary search over indices `0..peak`. If it returns a valid index we return it, because the left side holds the smaller indices. Otherwise we run a descending binary search over indices `peak + 1..n - 1`, where the comparisons are reversed: `key < arr[mid]` moves `start = mid + 1` and `key > arr[mid]` moves `end = mid - 1`. For example, the descending search uses `if (key == arr[mid]) return mid; else if (key < arr[mid]) start = mid + 1; else end = mid - 1;`.

Returning the left-side match first naturally yields the smaller index when the key exists on both the rising and falling sides. Each of the three phases, finding the peak and the two searches, is logarithmic, so the whole algorithm is logarithmic.

A senior nuance is that the descending search is just an ordinary binary search with the inequality signs flipped, so reusing a single order-aware search routine keeps the code clean. Another nuance is correctly partitioning at the peak so neither search overlaps the other. Complexity is O(log n) time and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores the intraday price of Rajesh's stock as a bitonic series, and compliance asks at which earliest point the price reached a specific value. This is exactly how Search Bitonic Array works: locate the key in a rise-then-fall array, preferring the earlier occurrence.

Problem 2 — A linear scan is too slow for long series, and a naive binary search fails because the array is not monotonic. This is why we first find the peak to split the series into two monotonic halves and binary-search each with the correct order.

The code defines a `BitonicSearchService` exposing `firstIndexOf(prices, key)` returning the earliest index or minus one. A `Demo` searches a bitonic price series for a value present on both sides and logs the earlier index.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: prices 101, 119, 140, 135, 119, 104 and key 119.

Step 1: Find the peak. Comparisons converge to index 2, value 140, the high.

Step 2: Ascending search over indices 0 to 2. mid is 1, price at 1 is 119 which equals the key, so we return index 1 immediately.

Step 3: Because the rising side matched, we never search the falling side, so the earlier index 1 is returned even though 119 also appears at index 4.


sections.s6_takeaway:
Search Bitonic Array is a composite Modified Binary Search problem. Because the array first rises and then falls, it is not globally monotonic, so a single binary search fails. My first move is to find the peak index using the slope comparison, where I compare each middle element with its right neighbour. That peak splits the array into a clean ascending half on the left and a clean descending half on the right.

Then I binary-search the ascending half with the usual comparisons, and if the key is not there I binary-search the descending half with the inequality signs reversed. I search the rising half first on purpose, because when the key appears on both sides the rising half holds the smaller index, so returning its match first gives the earliest occurrence. I keep both searches in one order-aware routine driven by a boolean so I am not duplicating logic.

At the National Bank of India I used this against the intraday price series of Rajesh's stock, stored as a bitonic series, when compliance asked at which earliest point in the day the price reached a specific value. I found the daily high to split the series, searched the rising half, and only searched the falling half if needed, returning the earlier index, all in logarithmic time. Explaining the peak split, the reversed comparisons on the descending side, and the left-first rule for the smaller index is what shows an interviewer I can compose two binary-search variants correctly.
